3. AI for Data Analytics

November 18, 2026

GPT 6.2 is fresh out of the data center, and here are Data Analysis Benchmarks by Plotly https://plotly.com/blog/gpt-6-2-sol-plotly-data-analytics-bench/

I applaud the great analytics done on AI models in this blog post. We are now using AI to do Analytics about using AI for Analytics. This is a great read and I believe essential reading for all data folks today.

So, the famous Python library plotly maintains this 43 question secret analytics exam and GPT 6.2, SOTA as of 11/17/26, just passed the exam with 93% or 40/43 for $1.22. It's the fastest A-grade model and the 3rd cheapest for their exam. I'd be curious to take the test myself, but it is not public because naturally, the AIs could train on the benchmark easily. Side note, one instance of AI models tuning to common benchmarks might be Simon Willison's pelican on a bike drawing over on the HN forums.

Overall, the take-away from Plotly is that these models seem to be getting faster (10.5 seconds per question), and cheaper, with a 43 question exam costing only $1.22. The models were doing these fast analytics on a 19.9 M row data warehouse spanning 44 tables and 554 columns, 11 seconds per question: It's quite a performance!

I look forward to gauging the performance of these new models for AI-assisted development on White Oak Research. I am also going to incorporate Claude Code for some different takes on the CodeX analyses being produced thus far. With such an array of choices of model, it's important to stay curious and try broadly. I hope to review open models as well, since moving beyond the 2 biggest industry players in LLMs is going to be an interesting development in healthcare technology. Will we see coalescence into Claude and OpenAI, or will some orgs stand up their own internal LLMs based on Open Source systems?

1. LLMs and Medical Diagnoses

November 17, 2026

Do humans diagnose illnesses better with LLMs? I present here two different takes on the question.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02545-1

A fascinating study came out in March 2026, with an RCT of 70 internal medicine specialists. The research compares using an AI system as first or second opinion vs using "Conventional Resources" like Google or PubMed. Overall, they found that AI may helped in diagnostics slightly, and that Conventional Resources scored slightly lower than AI alone or AI+human collaborations.

To me, this research highlights the collaboration of AI and Human Clinicians. However, I do want to circle back to those Conventional Resources like PubMed and Google Search as comparators. This research study may be highlighting some of the UI/UX issues and lesser capabilities of those older "conventional" resources. Much has been made elsewhere of the story of internet search, ads, and how quality often suffers over time in these tools. Side note: will AI quality hold up long-term better than Google search?

In any case, there has been an opening for better Search to gain huge market share as simple fact-finders. Models may also provide reasoning and deal with complex interactions of multiple variables. A skillful AI user will manipulate model choice and effort-selector on a case-by-case basis, offering a better Google or a more advanced analytic workflow.

One interesting aspect of the study was its survey of clinicians, who found they are more likely to agree with the statement "I am open to using AI to help with complex clinical reasoning". Thus, LLMs are being considered in the clinic today and may be tried in clinics in the near future.

But wait! There's more. A second article appears.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04074-y

This other study of laypeople showed that LLMs may not have been better than conventional resources at aiding with diagnostics. I will note this was laypeople and they used ChatGPT 4o which is now a somewhat older AI model, and is markedly less powerful than November 2026 state of the art models. Whether or not the moving target of AI performance in real time actually stayed the same throughout trials, and whether these configurable AI services were used adeptly, there is certainly disagreement in medicine about the potential future for LLMs assisting in medicine.

Further study is needed soon, since there are medical, ethical, and yes financial incentives for it to be useful in improving healthcare outcomes. I expect to hear much more about AI in healthcare settings over the coming years. For now, it may be wise to raise awareness about LLMs and other kinds of statistical model, and perhaps provide training in schools about these models.

0. Why Write?

November 14, 2026

As a researcher and analyst, a creator of content ultimately, this is a strange time. While the cost of making new content has become lower than ever, we've seen a deluge of billions of ways to spend our attention. Now that AI can produce images, videos, music, writing, analytics, and the very code that is software and even AI, well, we humans might start to feel like the waters are rising.

In such a time, we must not stand still, but zoom out and critically think about this noisy landscape of content. While I may contribute some content-water here, as the Analytics on this website reflect the power of AI-assisted Development, I will hand-write blog entries the old-fashioned way, on a Bluetooth Ergonomic Keyboard.

I posit this truism: that the powers of LLMs are unlocked by the prompts of its intentioned users. For now, these users are humans with missions and goals and drives to produce value for humans. Yet in our quest for value-production, amidst all this amazing content, we are unable to take true rest for ourselves. We are tired out, and we feel we have less opportunity than we'd like to practice many pursuits and skills. Thus, naturally, less attention is now paid to writing skills than it was in recent decades.

Why write? Firstly, writing develops the mind's capacity to think, it is a meta-technology that helps the writer think better about the world. Secondly, those thoughts when well-written may become valuable to others, contributing to our community of human thought. Writing well helps us connect the dots to seek areas of consensus and coalescence with fellow minds. And elephant in the room: writing well helps us interface with AI and LLMs, thus improving our steering ability on the very-fast-moving AI ship. Lastly, it's fun and interesting to write, though it's less-so now as rusty as I am.

Thanks so much for reading. I look forward to writing my thoughts here, guaranteed 100% Homo Sapiens, giving you purely human takes via purely human-written essays.
